 Hon'Ble Mr. Justice Arun Monga
Order(Oral) 10/07/2024
1.

The matter pertains to an incident which occurred in the year 1999 for alleged offences under Sections 18(C)/27(B)(11), 22(1) (CCA)/22(3), 18-A/28, 27(D), 27(B)(1) & 18(A)(1) & 17(B)(D) of Drugs & Cosmetics Act and the present criminal revision petition has been pending since 2006.
2. Petitioner is assailing the legality and validity of the judgment/order dated 05.06.2006 passed by learned Sessions Judge, Jalore in Criminal Appeal No.15/2004, whereby the judgment/order dated 15.07.2004 passed by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jalore in Criminal Regular Case No.396/1999, convicting the revisionist-petitioners was upheld.

The petitioner was convicted and sentenced as under:-
 Offence u/s. Sentence Fine Default  18(C)/27(B)(11) of Drugs 01-year S.I. Rs.500/- 15 days S.I.
 & Cosmetics Act  22(1)(CCA)/22(3) of 3 months' S.I. - -
Drugs & Cosmetics Act  18-A/28 of Drugs& 3 months' S.I. - -
Cosmetics Act  27(D) of Drugs& 1 year S.I. Rs.500/- 15 days' S.I.
 Cosmetics Act  27(B)(1) of Drugs & 1 Year S.I. Rs.500/- 15 days' S.I.

I have heard the learned counsel for the revision-petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor and perused the case file.

4. At the very outset, instead of addressing the arguments on the merits of the conviction and the sentence awarded to the petitioner, learned counsel for the petitioner seeks concession of probation under Section 18 of the Probation of Offenders Act.

5. In support of his arguments, he relies on a judgment rendered by this Court in the case of State of Rajasthan Vs. Subhash Chandra &Ors. (S.B. Criminal Revision No.648/2017) decided on 31.07.2017, the relevant part of which reads as follows:
"In the case at hand, the respondents were held guilty for the offence under Section 27D of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 which carries a minimum sentence of one year with a proviso that in case the Court so feels, for adequate and special reasons to be recorded in the judgment, it may impose sentence for a term lesser than one year.

entities.text: State of Rajasthan Vs. Subhash Chandra &Ors. (S.B. Criminal Revision No.648/2017)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, apparently minimum sentence of one year provided for the offence under Section 27D of the Act is not absolute and discretion has been left with the Court to impose a lesser sentence albeit after recording adequate and special reasons.
It is further relevant to mention here that there is no specific provision in the Drugs and Cosmetics Act which bars applicability of Probation of Offenders Act.

Apparently, the observations made in paras 9 and 10 in the case of Bahubali would be very relevant in which it was laid down that benefit of probation could be claimed by offenders other than those found guilty for the offence with death or life imprisonment unless the operation of Probation of Offenders Act is excluded by statute.

Section 18 of the Probation of Offenders Act excludes applicability of the Act to section 31 of the Reformatory Schools Act, 1897, or sub- section (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 or of any law in force in any State relating to juvenile offenders or Borstal Schools.

In case of offence under any special Act enacted after the Probation of Offenders Act which prescribes minimum sentence, the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act cannot be invoked if the Special Act contains any excluding provision like Section 43 of the Defence of India Act.
There are subsequent enactments like N.D.P.S. Act and Prevention of Food Adulteration Act etc.

[2024:RJ-JD:28159] (3 of 3) [CRLR-522/2006] However, there is no specific provision in Drugs and Cosmetics Act which rules out applicability of Probation of Offenders Act and no such amendment appears to have been introduced in the Act till the date the case in hand was decided.

In view of the discussion made herein above, I am of the view that the trial Judge committed no error or illegality in extending benefit of Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act to the respondents after holding them guilty for the offence under Kana Ram vs State (2024:Rj-Jd:28159) on 10 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125853293/
2 ection 27D of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act by recording their plea of guilt and as a consequence, the Appellate Court was perfectly justified in rejecting the appeal preferred by the State of Rajasthan against the judgment of trial court.
The impugned judgments do not suffer from any shortcoming either factual or legal so as to warrant interference.

In view of the discussion made hereinabove, I find no reason to interfere in this revision which is hereby dismissed as being devoid of merit and also as being time barred."
6.
I am in respectful agreement with the views expressed in the aforesaid judgment.

Taking a cue from the same, I am of the opinion that in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, as well,
the petitioner is entitled to be released on probation.
7. Accordingly, the instant revision petition is partly allowed.

While the conviction of the petitioner is upheld, the sentence awarded is modified to the extent that he shall be released on probation under Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, on the conditions to be imposed by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jalore to his satisfaction.
For this purpose, the petitioner shall appear before the learned CJM, Jalore within four weeks along with a web print of this order.
8. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

(ARUN MONGA), J 13-/Jitender//-
